name: Galileo's Inclined Plane
statement: By rolling balls down a ramp to slow their fall, Galileo found the distance grows as the square of the time.
statementAccent: the distance grows as the square of the time
meaning: Galileo's inclined plane experiments were a series of investigations by the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei in the early seventeenth century, in which he rolled balls down smooth, gently sloping ramps to study how objects accelerate, and which established the mathematical law of falling bodies. Galileo could not directly time a freely falling object with the crude clocks of his day, so he diluted gravity by letting a ball roll down an inclined plane, slowing the motion enough to measure. His key notes date to around 1603 to 1604, and he published the results in his final book, Two New Sciences, in 1638. He found that the distance a ball travels from rest is proportional to the square of the time elapsed, the times-squared law, which means the motion is one of uniform, constant acceleration. He also found that this acceleration does not depend on the weight or mass of the ball, so that, absent air resistance, all bodies fall at the same rate. These findings overturned the long-accepted Aristotelian doctrine that heavier objects fall proportionally faster, and they laid the groundwork for the science of motion later completed by Newton.
mechanism: The experiments worked by slowing free fall to a measurable pace and finding the mathematical pattern in the motion. Galileo built a long, straight wooden beam with a smooth, straight channel cut along it, in which a hard, polished bronze ball could roll with little friction, and he propped one end up to make a gentle incline. Because the ball rolls down only the slope, it accelerates far more slowly than it would in free fall, giving him time to measure. Lacking an accurate clock, he timed the descents with a water clock, collecting and weighing the water that flowed out during each roll, so that equal weights of water marked equal intervals of time. Releasing the ball from rest and measuring how far it travelled in successive equal times, he found that the distances covered grew as the odd numbers one, three, five, seven, so that the total distance from the start was proportional to the square of the elapsed time. This times-squared relationship is the signature of uniform acceleration. By repeating the measurements at different slopes and, he reported, a hundred times over, and finding the same law, and that the result did not depend on the ball's weight, he established the law of naturally accelerated motion.

examples.text: Rolling a ball down a gentle ramp slowed its fall enough to time with a water clock, letting Galileo study acceleration.
In successive equal times the ball covered distances in the ratio one, three, five, seven, so the total grew as the square of the time.
The acceleration was the same regardless of the ball's weight, so absent air resistance all bodies fall at the same rate.

variants.name: The times-squared law
variants.text: The finding that distance from rest is proportional to the square of the elapsed time, the mark of uniform acceleration.

variants.name: Independence from mass
variants.text: The result that the rate of fall does not depend on the object's weight, overturning Aristotle's doctrine.

whyItMatters: Galileo's inclined plane experiments are foundational to modern physics because they established, by measurement and mathematics, the law governing how objects fall, replacing centuries of Aristotelian assumption with quantitative science. By showing that the distance fallen from rest grows as the square of the time, and that this acceleration is uniform and independent of an object's weight, Galileo overturned the ancient belief that heavier bodies fall proportionally faster and laid the empirical foundation for the science of motion that Isaac Newton would complete. Beyond the specific law, the experiments are celebrated as an early and exemplary use of the scientific method, combining a clever experimental design to make an unmeasurable motion measurable with a mathematical description of the results and repeated testing. They mark a turning point from qualitative natural philosophy to the mathematical, experimental physics that followed. The clarity of the times-squared law and the striking claim that all bodies fall alike made the work a model of how nature can be captured in mathematics.

working.text: let a polished ball roll down a gently inclined grooved beam so it accelerates slowly enough to measure.
measure the time of each roll with a water clock, marking equal intervals by equal weights of water.
observe that distance from rest grows as the square of the time, and is the same whatever the ball's weight.

limits: Galileo's inclined plane experiments are rightly foundational, but a few points deserve care. The dating should distinguish his working notes, usually placed around 1603 to 1604, from the publication of the results in Two New Sciences in 1638. The law that all bodies fall at the same rate holds only in the absence of air resistance, an idealization that Galileo reasoned toward rather than achieving perfectly, since real objects are slowed by the air. The famous story of Galileo dropping objects from the Leaning Tower of Pisa is not documented in his own writings and comes from a biography by his student Viviani written decades later, so it is widely regarded as legendary; the inclined plane experiments are the real, documented work and should not be conflated with the tower legend. His timing with a water clock was necessarily approximate.
misreadings: Galileo's law that all bodies fall at the same rate is not contradicted by a feather falling slower than a stone, since that difference is due to air resistance, which the law sets aside. The famous Leaning Tower of Pisa drop is likely a legend from a later biography, not documented fact, and is not the inclined plane experiments themselves. And his working notes of about 1603 to 1604 predate the 1638 publication of Two New Sciences, so treating air-resistance effects as refuting the law, the tower story as history, or the publication date as the date of discovery, misreads Galileo's documented inclined plane work.
origin: A series of experiments by Galileo Galilei in the early seventeenth century, with working notes around 1603 to 1604 and published in Two New Sciences in 1638, rolling balls down ramps to establish the times-squared law of uniformly accelerated falling motion.
